items.headline: Five EU countries announce migrant deportation centre in Rwanda
items.blurb: Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands have announced a "return hub" for failed asylum seekers.
items.text: Five EU countries will open a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda next year as part of a broader push to boost removals. Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands are expected to open a "return hub" ready to accept transfers in 2027, the Dutch and Danish governments announced in statements. The countries said the scheme would apply to migrants staying illegally in their nations who are subject to deportation, with the Dutch government adding it will provide an alternative if deportees cannot be returned to their country of origin. Deportees will be able to either integrate into Rwandan society or return to their home country, the nations said. The scheme will apply to people who have exhausted their legal avenues to stay in the five nations - unlike a scrapped British deal that envisaged sending people to Rwanda to have their claims processed. Legal challenges meant the UK deal never took off, and it was eventually junked by the incoming Labour government in 2024 . items.headline: Yemen army reports 661 attacks on Houthis amid Houthi push towards Aden
items.blurb: Yemen's army reports 173 Houthi fighters killed or wounded as government forces reposition to defend Aden.
items.text: Yemen’s army has said it carried out 661 attacks against Houthi positions across several fronts, killing or wounding 173 fighters, as government forces continue their military campaign amid Houthi territorial gains in the country’s southwest. Military spokesperson Colonel Majed al-Nuzaili said on Monday that the operations, conducted as part of the ongoing “Dawn of Yemen” offensive, included 15 air strikes, 526 artillery attacks, 53 drone strikes and 67 rocket attacks. In a statement on X, al-Nuzaili said the attacks had destroyed or damaged 71 military vehicles and pieces of equipment, as well as command-and-control centres, observation posts and fortifications. He said government forces, backed by the Popular Resistance, were continuing to confront Houthi movements in the provinces of Taiz, Marib and al-Jawf, while operations were also under way on southern fronts. The military said it would continue its offensive until it achieved its objectives, while taking precautions to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure. items.text: Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’ Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”. The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country. In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”. items.headline: Houthi rebel advance in Yemen may further destabilise global economy
items.blurb: The Iran-backed Houthis are gaining ground and their advance could have dangerous consequences, writes the BBC's security correspondent.
items.text: The Iran-backed Houthi rebels who seized much of Yemen in 2014 have now forced the army of the internationally recognised government to withdraw from the Red Sea coast in order to defend their interim capital, Aden. Their advance bodes ill for Yemen's legitimate, internationally recognised government, its Saudi backers and, by extension, much of the rest of the world. Yemen, a mountainous, heavily armed, intensely tribal and largely impoverished nation, sits at the far south-west corner of the Arabian Peninsula. The country has two coasts: One faces the Indian Ocean on which sits the once-prosperous trading port of Aden, the other faces the Red Sea and, most importantly, the narrow chokepoint at the southern exit of that waterway - the so-called Bab al-Mandab Strait or, in English, The Gate of Tears. Whoever controls that strait can threaten any or all maritime traffic passing through from both the Mediterranean and the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean. items.headline: Irish court jails man for life over Dublin knife attack that sparked riots
items.blurb: Three children and a woman were injured in the attack outside a central Dublin school in 2023.
items.text: A 52-year-old man has been sentenced to life behind bars for the attempted murder of three children in Dublin on November 23, 2023, in an attack that triggered rioting and looting in the Irish capital. Riad Bouchaker, an Algerian national and Irish citizen, was sentenced at the Central Criminal Court in Dublin on Monday after being found guilty in July on eight charges arising from the knife attack outside a school nearly three years ago. His victims included a five-year-old girl, a six-year-old girl, a five-year-old boy and a woman in her mid-30s. The youngest girl was stabbed in the heart, resulting in severe disability after her brain was deprived of oxygen for 40 minutes following the attack. The girl, who is now eight, cannot speak and communicates only by blinking. She uses a wheelchair and is fed through a tube in her stomach because she is unable to swallow safely. items.headline: US basketball player arrested with 75lb of marijuana at Nigerian airport, say authorities
items.blurb: Suspect named as Greene Da’monte Khiree Drug smuggling carries life sentence in Nigeria An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly attempting to smuggle 33.95kg (75lb) of marijuana into the country.
items.text: An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly attempting to smuggle 33.95kg (75lb) of marijuana into the country. Nigeria’s National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said a 28-year-old player named as Greene Da’monte Khiree from the state of Georgia was arrested at Lagos’s main airport last Wednesday after he arrived on a flight from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates. The NDLEA said the player told them he had come to Nigeria to “build networks” for his basketball career. The agency said evidence on his phone suggested he had “knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity”. The NDLEA said it detained the player when he attempted to leave the airport with his hand luggage after abandoning two checked-in bags. The agency said those two bags were found to contain 32 parcels of marijuana, and a tracking device. Nigeria has strict drug laws, and trafficking carries a sentence of life in prison. A basketball player by the name of Damonte Greene is listed on the roster of the Pattani Raptors in the Thai Premier Men’s League.

items.text: Nvidia has dismissed a campaign calling for Jensen Huang to be handed back his job as allies, including US President Donald Trump, backed the effort. Trump said on Monday that he "would certainly not mind" if Huang was reinstated, adding to a list of supporters who are backing a "Bring Jensen Back" campaign. Fellow tech bosses, including SpaceX's Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, chief executive of Fortnite-maker Epic Games, have also supported Huang's return. But the BBC has been told the board of the AI chip giant is not interested in bringing him back after he resigned last week following revelations he had two affairs, including one that involved a suspected Chinese spy. Meanwhile on Monday, the Trump administration said it will further restrict China's ​access to AI chips from companies like Nvidia. The reported affairs created a crisis for one of the world's most valuable firms - a central company in AI and the US battle against China for dominance. items.blurb: Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to…
items.text: Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city. The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved. The growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result. Meanwhile, a heated debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger and in some cases need to be relocated. items.headline: Landmark Crimea bridge hit as Russia reports biggest Ukrainian drone attack of war
items.blurb: Russia said Ukraine had launched over 2,000 drones over the course of a day, while Kyiv came under a record 17 air raid alerts.
items.text: Russia says it has recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, in which a landmark bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea sustained minor damage and several oil refineries were hit. The Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin added. Kyiv, meanwhile, came under a record 17 air raid alerts in a single day. At least seven people were killed by Russian strikes and attacks on energy infrastructure caused blackouts for 50,000 people. The intense strikes come days after US, Ukrainian and Russian envoys held talks aimed at ending the war. The war in Ukraine began with Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that drones had struck the Crimean Bridge connecting Russia with the annexed peninsula, leading to traffic restrictions. items.headline: Cyclone Akvan brews over Bay of Bengal: What you need to know
items.blurb: Cyclone Akvan, a severe storm developing in the Bay of Bengal, is expected to intensify from a depression into a cyclonic storm this week; what to know.
items.text: Cyclone Akvan would be the third cyclone to hit A.P. in a month if it makes landfall. File | Photo Credit: KOMMURI SRINIVAS A weather system brewing over the Bay of Bengal is expected to intensify into a severe cyclonic storm over the coming days, according to the Indian Meteorological Department (IMD). The system has intensified into a Cyclonic Storm on Monday (November 16, 2026) evening, and is moving north-northwestwards towards Andhra Pradesh and has been named ‘Akvan’, a name suggested by Iran under the North Indian Ocean naming list. It originated as a well-marked low-pressure area over the southeast Bay of Bengal on Saturday (November 14, 2026), the system intensified into a depression by Sunday (November 15, 2026) morning. The storm may continue to move north-northwestwards and intensify into a Severe Cyclonic Storm over westcentral Bay of Bengal by Tuesday (November 17, 2026) evening and may cross the A.P. coast around noon on November 20, as a Very Severe Cyclonic Storm, with windspeed gusting to 145 kmph, similar to that of Arnab. items.headline: Congress forms screening committees for five poll-bound states
items.text: The Congress on Monday constituted screening committees for five states going to the Assembly polls in early 2027, with AICC national treasurer Ajay Maken appointed chairperson of the panel for Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra Congress in-charge Sirivella Prasad named to head the committee of Punjab. The five poll-bound states include UP, Punjab, Uttarakhand, Goa and Manipur, where Assembly elections are scheduled in the first quarter of 2027. The committees will scrutinise panels of probable candidates submitted by the respective state election committees, shortlist names and forward them to the party’s Central Election Committee, which will take the final decision on candidates for each state. Maken’s committee for UP will include Aslam Shaikh and BV Srinivas. The Congress is in an alliance with SP in the state, where seat-sharing arrangements for the Assembly polls are yet to be finalised. Prasad’s committee for Punjab will have AICC secretaries Sachin Sawant and Nivedith Alva as members. The development comes two days after SP chief Akhilesh Yadav said at the 24th Hindustan Times Leadership Summit that the Congress had asked for 181 out of the 403 assembly seats. Asked if the Congress had asked for 200 seats, Yadav had said, “Slightly less than that”. Asked if they had sought 180, he said: “Add one to 180”. “ Samajwadi Party and us have made up our mind on how many seats we will contest. INDIA coalition will together defeat the BJP,” he had added. “Our relationship with the Congress party is very good.” HT learns the Congress – which fought the 2022 elections alone and won just two seats, compared to the SP’s 111 – submitted its wishlist on October 19. items.headline: Let’s work to get back to 1.5° C target: COP31 draft agreement
items.text: At the start of the second week of negotiations at the ongoing climate conference in the Turkish city of Antalya, host countries Turkey and Australia circulated the first draft of a cover decision that expresses deep concern at the scientific finding that the 1.5 degree Celsius target had gone beyond reach and urges every country to work harder to limit the magnitude and duration of temperature overshoot beyond that target. The 18-page draft decision, which is likely to undergo several amendments, also calls upon countries pursue efforts to bring back the levels of global warming to within 1.5 degree Celsius “as early as possible within this century”. The COP31 climate meeting in Antalya is being held in the backdrop of recent scientific assessments that it was no longer possible for the world to limit the rise in global temperatures to within 1.5 degree Celsius from pre-industrial times, one of the key objectives of the 2015 Paris Agreement. The bodies of six Liangmai Naga civilians were laid to rest in Manipur’s Kangpokpi district on Monday (November 16, 2026), 187 days after they were abducted and subsequently killed almost a month later. The family of the deceased and Naga organisations had refused to claim the bodies — kept at the mortuary of the Jawaharlal Nehru Institute of Medical Sciences in Imphal since June 10 — until their demands were met. items.headline: May agree to disagree in democracy, but commitment to Constitution must: Vice President CP Radhakrishnan
items.text: Citing “disruption” as a ma­jor issue in Parliament and Assemblies these days, Vice-President C P Radhakrishnan Monday said debates, discus­sions, or even disruption must lead to better decision-making. Addressing the Odisha Legislative Assembly, Radhakrishnan emphasised that differences of opinion should not come in the way of the larger commitment to the people and the Constitution. “A major issue we face nowadays inside Parliament and assemblies is disruption due to differences of opinion across the floor. In a democracy, we may agree to disagree, but we should remember one thing — our commitment to the people and the Constitution,” he said. Radhakrishnan said debate strengthens democracy while constructive cooperation advances the state and the nation. Sujit Bisoyi is a Special Correspondent with the Indian Express and covers Odisha. items.text: Amid reports that ousted CEO Jensen Huang is in talks with close allies about a potential return to the helm of the world's second-most valuable company, the Nvidia board is focused on its investigation into the co-founder’s ties to an alleged Chinese spy. Citing unnamed sources, CNBC also reported that Nvidia’s board of directors had not discussed bringing back Huang, who announced his resignation on November 12. Last week, Nvidia’s board had announced that they have hired law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct an investigation into whether company secrets or national security were compromised, after Huang admitted to having an affair with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based Chinese business executive. On Friday, the board also said it was still selecting a search firm to find a new CEO for the company, adding that it had not formally engaged any potential candidates. However, the Financial Times reported that Nvidia’s board has approached British chipmaker Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas in its search for a potential successor to Huang. items.headline: 'Complete system reset' needed to get 440,000 young people into work, says major review
items.blurb: Alan Milburn's review will call for sweeping reforms to the education, work and welfare systems.
items.text: Sweeping reforms are needed to help 440,000 more young people into work, according to former minister Alan Milburn. Almost one million young people aged 16 to 24 in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet" - a current rate of 13%, which Milburn wants to fall to around 5% within a decade. His government-commissioned review, due to be published in full on Tuesday, calls for ministers to intervene from early childhood through to adulthood, funded in part by radical changes to benefits for young adults. But Helen Whately, Conservative shadow work and pensions secretary, said Milburn's proposals were in parts "too cautious" and too reliant on the "expensive hand of the state". Many of the review's proposed changes are specific to England, with some welfare and tax measures applying across all home nations. Milburn, a former Labour health secretary, says extensive change is needed to avoid a "lost generation", and address what he describes as a "moral" crisis. items.blurb: The share sale will open to institutional and retail investors on 19 November and close on 23 November, with a stock market listing expected on 27 November.
items.text: Mahanadi Coalfields Ltd, Coal India Ltd's largest coal-producing subsidiary, has set a price band of ₹ 129–136 per share for its initial public offering (IPO), seeking a valuation of up to ₹ 90,000 crore ($9.6 billion) in what will be the largest listing of a state-owned entity this year. The share sale will open to institutional and retail investors on 19 November and close on 23 November, with a stock market listing expected on 27 November. The offering comprises an offer for sale (OFS) of 661.8 million shares, representing a 10% stake, by parent Coal India . At the upper end of the price band, the transaction is expected to raise ₹ 8,981 crore ($955 million). Since no fresh shares are being issued, Mahanadi Coalfields will not receive any proceeds from the IPO, with the entire amount accruing to Coal India. Mahanadi's IPO marks the third stock market listing of a Coal India subsidiary in 2026, as the central government steps up efforts to monetize state-owned assets. In a regulatory filing, the company said its fundraise committee approved the opening of the issue on November 16, along with the preliminary placement document. The QIP is part of the company's proposed fundraise of up to Rs 2,500 crore, which was approved by its board on October 16, 2026. Shareholders subsequently cleared the proposal through a special resolution passed via postal ballot. The floor price has been determined in accordance with the pricing formula prescribed under SEBI's Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements (ICDR) Regulations. Urban Company may offer a discount of up to 5% on the floor price, with the final issue price to be decided in consultation with the book running lead managers. items.headline: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
items.blurb: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t.
items.text: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors. For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses. AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built. We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. items.headline: Building AI that can work across the enterprise
items.blurb: For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate.
items.text: For years, enterprises have approached AI as a series of discrete experiments. Now, as AI agents begin to move into the workflows that run the business, that model is starting to look inadequate. Organizations moving from isolated pilots toward AI agents and autonomous workflows are confronting a deeper challenge: rethinking how data, business processes, governance, and people fit together, turning AI from a collection of tools into part of the enterprise operating model. For Thorsten Leiduck, SVP and global head of SAP Business AI Platform Ecosystem, that shift begins with treating AI as an enterprise platform rather than a collection of disconnected projects. “AI is absolutely dependent on the data foundation,” he says, arguing that companies need a connected, semantically rich layer that reflects their business before they can reliably deploy AI across processes. The stakes also change as AI moves into mission-critical workflows. items.blurb: The FBI says that the open source hacking tool was used in cyberattacks targeting a U.S. IT giant and the South Korean financial industry.
items.text: The FBI is warning that hackers are relying on autonomous AI hacking tools to launch cyberattacks across the U.S. and globally. The campaigns include a widespread hack of customers of American IT company ConnectWise and across South Korea’s financial industry. In its latest flash cybersecurity advisory , the FBI says hackers have targeted several industries in recent months, including financial services, government, tech, defense, phone and internet companies, and law firms, using open source tools like Artex to carry out autonomous-driven cyberattacks. Artex is one of several open source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network’s defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be “noisy,” meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company’s defensive alerts. There are four categories of limited usage, MacRumors reports, including using Siri AI for “multi-step, personal context requests,” image generation and editing tools, automations in Shortcuts that “rely on Apple Foundation Cloud and Cloud Pro Models,” and third-party apps that use those same cloud models. Apple hasn’t specified exactly how many times those features and tools can be used each day before limits are reached, but they’ll vary based on the task. items.text: Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen . These names are less descriptive than the Pro/Flash monikers of earlier releases, but Hydrogen’s purpose is clear: It replaces the faster, more economical Flash models most people in Google’s ecosystem use. Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it’s 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces “fabricated claims” by more than 5x, according to Google’s analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash’s score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon. Google believes Hydrogen will be a key part of how developers work with agentic coding tools. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world. These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. items.text: OpenAI is facing a new lawsuit from the California Attorney General’s office , alleging that the company’s training practices and lax security pose an ongoing danger to the public. At the center of the case is the July 2026 Hugging Face compromise , in which a pre-release model within OpenAI compromised both companies’ security systems to complete a training benchmark. In its official report on the incident , OpenAI called it “an outlier scenario involving a rare and unexpected confluence of events.” The California lawsuit represents one of the first attempts by a government regulator to hold an AI lab legally accountable for a rogue agent incident, with significant implications for both OpenAI’s competitors and its clients. The complaint centers on the Hugging Face incident, but also cites similar incidents involving RubyGems , DseWiki , the Wikimedia Foundation , and Australian government websites as evidence that the underlying behavior is ongoing. items.text: Three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corma has raised a $125 million Series A round at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA, the company said. Corma offers AI models and agents trained for cybersecurity defense. It has now raised a total of $185 million from backers, including Sequoia Capital, Khosla Ventures, and Coatue. Corma isn’t the only company using AI to play defense. Other examples include Kevin Mandia’s new startup Armadin , as well as Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and other established players, and too many other startups to count. Still, it’s a young market and a necessary one. Corma says it stands out from the crowd by being a frontier AI research lab focused on protection.

items.headline: Fractal Eyes AI Acquisitions Ahead Of Enterprise AI Scale-Up
items.blurb: Fractal Analytics is evaluating acquisitions across healthcare, agentic AI and AI engineering as it looks to strengthen its capabilities ahead…
items.text: Fractal Analytics is in talks with 20–25 startups for potential acquisitions across healthcare, agentic AI and AI engineering The acquisitions could strengthen Fractal’s enterprise AI capabilities, expand its access to specialised talent and improve its competitive positioning Fractal is open to deals worth up to ₹1,000 Cr, with a preferred acquisition size of $50–100 Mn, and reported cash and cash equivalents of ₹1,728 Cr as of September 30, 2026 Fractal Analytics is evaluating acquisitions across healthcare, agentic AI and AI engineering as it looks to strengthen its capabilities ahead of an expected scale-up in enterprise AI adoption. CEO Srikanth Velamakanni told Reuters that the company is in discussions with 20–25 startups for potential acquisitions. The M&A focus would be on gaining specialised engineering talent and strengthening its relationships with large cloud computing firms and frontier AI labs, particularly in areas where Fractal wants to build deeper capabilities.
